title: Deep Learning at National Taiwan University
paragraphs: From 2024 Q1 to Q2, I was allowed to train for two weeks each in emergency medicine and psychiatry at National Taiwan University, for a total of four weeks. First, as a premise, in the case of internal medicine, National Taiwan University's policy is not to give exchange students the authority to write charts nor allow them to be involved in practice, and it is basically observation only. In form, one basically joins a local students' polyclinic group and acts together with them. Also, emergency medicine cannot accept anyone who is not a Chinese speaker, and psychiatry accepts English too, but if you cannot speak Chinese, it seems you would spend two weeks as if thrown into a room of time and mind. (Just understanding Chinese is something we appreciate! In the past students who could not speak Chinese came. . . they understood nothing, so they really only watched. By psychiatry Dr. 謝明憲) However, in clinical departments bound by Chinese, I was actually able to have deep experiences that would have been impossible with English alone, and one could say I was able to do deep learning (?) at National Taiwan University.

The 14 days in emergency medicine consisted of listening to lectures tightly packed from morning to evening for only the first two days, and for the rest of the days, believe it or not, taking on-call shifts. One has to take 9 shifts per person: 3 day shifts (8:00-20:00), 2 night shifts (20:00-8:00), 2 evening shifts (12:00-20:00), 1 pediatric emergency evening shift (12:00-22:00) and 1 critical care area shift (8:00-20:00). Of course it had nothing to do with me (laughs). I was told that if I wanted to observe I could contact the members of the polyclinic group and ask someone to let me in, so I observed one day shift, one night shift and one critical care area shift. There were mainly two things that left an impression. The first was the tolerance toward medical acts by medical students. Although one needs to consult a senior doctor and obtain approval, from chart writing to prescribing, they were routinely made to deal with emergency patients alone. Perhaps because the local students were about to graduate (they graduate at the end of June and become residents from July 1), they were to insert NG (nasogastric tubes) and Foley (urinary catheters) themselves, and they were even entrusted with suturing a small wound around the eyebrow of a patient who had fallen from a motorbike. (I also wanted, if possible, to try at least a little helping, but after confirming many times, it turned out that exchange students are not allowed procedures (medical procedures) and cannot touch anything, only observe.) It was busy in any case, and medical students were treated as part of the workforce. The reason for this is said to lie in Taiwan's health insurance. Taiwan has a universal health insurance system as Japan does, but the referral-focused medical institution system that Japan has apparently does not function. For insured treatment, fees other than the first-visit fee are uniform, but the first-visit fee may be freely decided by each hospital. Clinics have high first-visit fees, and because university hospitals do not collect a selective-care fee, there are many patients who think it is better to visit a university hospital since the cost is no different, and as a result the whole hospital is busy in any case. In addition, because waiting times are relatively short and appointments are unnecessary, not a few people visit the emergency department as walk-ins even when it is not urgent. The second was less an impression than an experience, being allowed to ride in an ambulance. The supervising doctor, Dr. 張, seems to be something like a medical counsellor (?) for the Chungxiao Squad of the Taipei City Fire Department, and goes to the Chungxiao Squad once a month. That opportunity happened to come while I was rotating through emergency medicine, so I was allowed to accompany him. My dream (?) of riding in an ambulance for the first time in my life came true in Taiwan. After transporting the first patient to a nearby hospital, on the way back we were "dispatched online (線上派遣)" and took on a patient with OHCA (Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest), and we returned to National Taiwan University Hospital with a pale-skinned patient lying beside my seat fitted with a LUCAS (automated chest compression device) and an AED. It was an experience with great impact. Incidentally, I think the restriction of emergency medicine to "Chinese speakers only" is probably because the doctors are busy and have no leeway to look after trainees. If you are not a Chinese speaker, it seems it would be a rather painful experience.

Psychiatry was more low-key than emergency medicine, and the clerkship content was mainly conferences and rounds, with occasional outpatient observation and lectures. The content of the local students' clerkship was also mainly rounds and chart writing, and I got the impression that they had few opportunities to be involved in practice. In that respect, I personally think the edge goes to Nagoya University's present psychiatry clerkship, in which one is allowed to take preliminary histories several times. As an overall image, whether due to cultural differences I am not sure, but there were more patients with a history of suicide and patients with severe schizophrenia than in Japan. There were also many patients who spoke Taiwanese (the Taiwanese version of Hokkien), so during ward rounds I often could not follow the conversation. As part of the psychiatry clerkship, there was a visit to an outside hospital. The whole polyclinic group visited the Taipei City Hospital Songde Branch (branch hospital), a hospital specialised in psychiatry located at a corner of the Xinyi District, where Taipei 101 is. After listening to a lecture, we observed the wards, the seclusion rooms and the day service area. The day service area had its own character; besides wholesome (?) content similar to Japan's, such as cooking classes, craft classes, calligraphy classes and karaoke rooms, there was also a corner, unseen in Japan, where people were noisily playing mahjong. I was also allowed to see the large gymnasium in the basement with a basketball court and a tennis court, and a dance studio.

There were four things I thought were especially important through this study abroad. The first is that I got stimulation toward studying medicine. It is embarrassing to say, but I do not usually study much, and I think I only do Nagoya University's polyclinic clerkships reasonably seriously. However, when I trained together with the sixth-year students of National Taiwan University, who were suddenly entrusted with patients this time and would take the national exam and become residents in a few months, my own lack of study was thrown into relief, and I felt like "when you see a worthy person, think of equalling him" (見賢思斉焉). Also, since local students study medicine in English, I checked with a friend, "Then you can read USMLE questions too, right?", and the reply was "I understand the content itself (as far as the content goes)," so I secretly blushed, as I keep thinking of starting to study for the USMLE but have not set my hand to it. Several months after returning to Japan, with deep reflection, I am gradually making up for what I have not studied until now. The second is that I made local friends. Not only classmates at National Taiwan University but also teaching assistants (administrative staff who are not directly involved in practice or teaching, who "assist teaching") and senior doctors became friendly with me, and in a sense I was able to widen my network. I was also invited, "Taiwanese medicine uses English, so if you want to go to an English-speaking country in the future, come do a clerkship at NTU before that." Being able to have a connection with a place where I have almost no ties was also one of the meanings of the study abroad for me. The third is that I was able to think about digitalisation. I am an extreme digital person; I make reasonably good use of new functions of various devices and apps and usually prefer electronic materials to paper media, so I am more sensitive than most to digitalisation. Although I did not mention it in the preceding text, in fact Taiwan's medical information system is quite advanced, and with just one insurance card one can see practice information from other medical institutions, and one can access charts even from outside the hospital on one's own smartphone or computer. Of course, due to cultural differences and so on, ideas and common sense regarding the handling of personal information also differ, but the integration of practice information (multiple medical institutions, linkage with the insurance card) is worth emulating. At least, through this study abroad I learned that such a world (system) exists and is actually in operation. I thought I would keep it in a corner of my mind and make good use of this knowledge when the time comes. The fourth is that I was able to think about internationalisation. In Taiwan, chart entries and drug names were mostly in English. It may be only me, but having received medical education in Japan, I had arbitrarily assumed that in other countries too charts are written in the national language. Even before going to Taiwan I had desperately practised the zhuyin input method, an IME widely used in Taiwan (something like kana input versus romaji input in Japan), but in the end I could not write charts, and even if I could have, they were almost all in English (with some chief complaints, place names, hospital names and so on in Chinese), so the zhuyin input method had no occasion to be used. Drug names were also mostly in English. I thought it could not be helped if prescription drugs for hospital use were in English, but when I picked up over-the-counter drugs at the Matsumoto Kiyoshi under Taipei Station and looked at them, the ingredient lists written on the instructions, apart from Chinese herbal medicines, were also in English. What is more, the technical terms in Taiwan's national medical licensing exam are accompanied by English, and a friend said "Actually, since I don't understand the Chinese, I look at the English." Incidentally, Taiwanese medicine has been English-only since at least the 1950s, so it is apparently a historical custom. At first I thought Japanese medicine too should fully promote English and actively internationalise. The first move for that is, above all, to add English to the national medical licensing exam. Because I would not like the double work of wanting to study medicine in English and yet having to learn Japanese again to prepare for the national exam. But on closer investigation, I noticed that English is already given alongside in the national nursing licensing exam. When I wondered why only the nursing exam and not the physician exam, and thought about it carefully, one of the disadvantages that first came to mind was that if medical study were centred on English, it could lead to an outflow of doctors overseas, and the maldistribution of doctors, already bad, might worsen. Conversely, inflow from overseas could also bring about a surplus of doctors. In reality, various other factors are involved too, and it is just my personal thinking, but I was made to realise that my thinking was simplistic, that internationalisation should not be promoted without deep thought. Then, how far should "internationalisation" go, and where should it stop? What is the significance of becoming an "international" doctor? I have no choice but to keep thinking about it from now on.

Looking back, if I had not gone on this study abroad, I was able to have a very valuable once-in-a-lifetime experience that I would never have had. I troubled many more people than my classmates with application procedures and so on, but as a result I somehow managed to see it through and I am deeply moved. I would like to sincerely thank everyone on the staff of the International Research Office, beginning with Professor 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川, who supported me. Also, thanks equally to the teaching assistants of the office of the National Taiwan University College of Medicine, senior 張耀文, senior 曾文鴻, teaching assistant 盧愷儀 of emergency medicine, Dr. 張家銘, Squad Leader 陳 of the Chungxiao Squad of the Taipei City Fire Department, Dr. 謝明憲 of psychiatry, and my classmates in NTU M5 and M6. Special thanks also to teaching assistant 張以雯. I look forward to the day we meet again.
